title: Payday Loans, BNPL & Other Traps
description: Fast cash, weekly payments, and the price hidden in a small fee.
wolfLine: Fast cash is the most expensive money in the woods.

payday-loan.definition: A small, short loan due on your next payday. The fee looks tiny and the yearly cost is enormous.
payday-loan.example: Borrow $100 for two weeks and pay a $15 fee. That is about a 390% APR.

buy-now-pay-later.definition: A plan that splits a purchase into a few payments, often four. On time, interest is often $0. Miss one, and a fee can land. Several plans stack.
buy-now-pay-later.example: Four payments of $50 cover a $200 purchase. Three plans at once can mean $150 leaving your account in one week.

title-loan.definition: A short loan that uses your car title as collateral. Miss the payments and the lender can take the car.
title-loan.example: Borrow $1,000 against a car worth $8,000. The car is on the line for a $1,000 emergency.

lessons.title: Payday Loan Math
lessons.summary: Fifteen dollars on a hundred, for two weeks, is not a small price.

steps.context: A [[payday loan]] of $100 with a $15 fee, due in two weeks, does not look like much. There are 26 two-week periods in 52 weeks. 15% × 26 = 390% [[APR]].
steps.prompt: What is a payday loan?
choices: A small loan due on your next payday, with a fee that hides a huge yearly cost
A cheaper form of a credit card
An advance from your employer’s paycheck with no lender
steps.explain: The fee is the whole product.

steps.prompt: The fee is $15 on $100. What percent of the loan is the fee?
How many two-week periods are in a 52-week year?
What APR does 15% every two weeks work out to?
You roll the $100 loan four times, paying the $15 fee each time, and never cut the principal. How much have the fees cost?
steps.explain: $15 × 4 = $60, and you still owe the $100.

steps.prompt: A $15 fee on $100 is cheap because 15 is a small number.
steps.explain: For two weeks, that fee is about a 390% APR.

lessons.title: Rent to Own
lessons.summary: The weekly payment is the advertisement. The year of weeks is the price.

steps.context: Rent-to-own lets you take an item home for a weekly fee. You can pay several times the cash price before you own it.
steps.prompt: A laptop is $900 in cash, or $35 a week for 104 weeks. What do the weekly payments add up to?
How much more is that than the $900 cash price?
What are you mostly paying for?
choices: The right to spread a $900 item across two years, at a very high price
A warranty that cuts the price
steps.explain: Same laptop, $2,740 extra.

steps.prompt: Stopping the weekly payments usually means you own a share of the item.
steps.explain: In a typical rent-to-own deal you return it, and the payments you made do not buy you equity.

steps.prompt: You can save $45 a week. How many weeks to reach the $900 cash price?
steps.explain: $900 ÷ $45 = 20 weeks. Then you own it, for $900.

steps.prompt: Which is the careful path if the laptop can wait?
choices: Save $45 a week and buy it for $900
Put it on a payday loan
steps.explain: Twenty-six weeks of saving beats two years of fees.

lessons.title: Title Loans
lessons.summary: The loan is small. The collateral is your way to work.

steps.context: A [[title loan]] is secured by your car. Borrow $1,000 and the lender holds the title. Miss the payments and they can take a car worth far more than $1,000.
steps.prompt: What does a title loan use as collateral?
choices: A credit card you do not have
steps.explain: The car is how they get paid if you do not.

steps.prompt: The car is worth $8,000. The loan is $1,000. How much of the car’s value is at risk for that loan?
steps.explain: The whole car. They do not repossess $1,000 worth of it.

steps.prompt: Why is that a bad trade for a $1,000 emergency?
choices: You can lose an $8,000 car over a $1,000 debt
Title loans build a credit score for free
steps.explain: The collateral is oversized on purpose.

steps.prompt: Paying the title loan off on time means you get the title back.
steps.explain: The danger is the miss, not the paperwork itself.

steps.prompt: The fee is $25 per $100 borrowed, per month. On $1,000, what is one month’s fee?
steps.explain: $25 × 10 = $250. That is 25% in a single month.

steps.prompt: What is the thing you are really risking?
choices: The car you use to get to work
steps.explain: Easy to get is not easy to escape.

lessons.title: Buy Now, Pay Later
lessons.summary: Four small payments feel like zero. Three plans do not.

steps.context: [[Buy now, pay later]] splits a purchase, often into four payments. Pay on time and interest is often $0. A late payment can cost a fee, and the plans stack if you open several.
steps.prompt: A $200 purchase is split into 4 payments. How much is each payment, with no fee?
On-time buy-now-pay-later payments are often interest-free.
steps.explain: The trap is missing one, or opening too many.

steps.prompt: You miss a payment and the fee is $10. What did that “free” plan just cost, on top of the $50 you still owe?
steps.explain: The fee is $10. The $50 payment is still due too.

steps.prompt: Three plans want $45, $30, and $25 in the same week. How much leaves your account?
You have $80 that week. What is the problem?
choices: The plans want $100. You are $20 short
steps.explain: $100 − $80 = $20 short. That is how a pile of small plans becomes a late fee.

steps.prompt: When is buy now, pay later least dangerous?
choices: One plan, for something you needed, that fits the weeks you will pay it
Five plans for things you wanted
A plan you already cannot see how to pay
steps.explain: One at a time, and only if the payments are already in the budget.

lessons.title: “No Credit Check”
lessons.summary: The ad is loud because the price is the part they hope you will not do.

steps.context: “No credit check” means the lender is not using your [[credit score]] to price the loan. Payday loans, title loans, and some rent-to-own deals live here. The cost is in the fee.
steps.prompt: An offer says “no credit check.” What is that usually a sign of?
choices: A high price, because the lender is not using your score to set a fair rate
steps.explain: They are not skipping the check to be kind.

steps.prompt: No credit check means the loan cannot hurt you.
steps.explain: It can still take a fee, a car, or a chunk of your next paycheck.

steps.prompt: Which question matters more than “Will they approve me?”
choices: What do I pay back, in dollars, and what can they take?
How fast can I get the money
steps.explain: Approval is easy when the price is ugly.

steps.prompt: The ad: borrow $200, pay back $260 in two weeks. How much is the fee?
That $60 fee is what percent of the $200?
steps.explain: $60 ÷ $200 = 30%, for two weeks.

steps.prompt: What do you do with an offer that will not show the total you repay?
choices: Assume the total equals what you borrowed
steps.explain: If the total is hidden, the total is the product.

lessons.title: Spot the Trap
lessons.summary: The friendly line is not the expensive one.

steps.context: Read the ad as a receipt. What you receive and what you pay back are the only honest numbers.

doc.title: Payday ad
doc.subtitle: Due on your next payday
doc.note: The $260 already includes a $60 fee. The $25 is on top.

steps.prompt: Which line is an extra charge stacked on top of the $260 payoff?
steps.explain: The $25 “processing charge” sits on top of a payoff that already includes a $60 fee.

doc.title: Payday ad
doc.subtitle: Due on your next payday
doc.note: The $260 already includes a $60 fee. The $25 is on top.

steps.prompt: How much more than $200 do you pay if every line on this ad is real?

doc.title: Payday ad
doc.subtitle: Due on your next payday
doc.note: The $260 already includes a $60 fee. The $25 is on top.

steps.prompt: What do you hand over in 14 days?
What did “no credit check” cost you here?
steps.explain: $85 ÷ $200 = 42.5% in two weeks.

steps.prompt: A processing charge in the fine print is optional if you did not notice it.
steps.explain: If it is on the paper you sign, it is in the deal.

steps.prompt: What would a fair ad lead with?
steps.explain: Dollars in, dollars out.

lessons.title: Better Options When You Are Short
lessons.summary: Slow help is usually cheaper than fast cash.

steps.context: When cash is short, the order is: billers and a payment plan, then anything you can sell or pause, then a credit union or a person who will not take your car. A payday loan is the last door, not the first.
steps.prompt: A $150 bill is due and you are short. What is worth trying before a payday loan?
choices: Ask the biller for a payment date, and cut or pause something else
A second payday loan to pay the first
steps.explain: A biller would often rather get the money late than not at all.

steps.prompt: You pause a $40 subscription and sell a $90 item you do not use. How much of a $150 gap does that close?
How much of the $150 is still short?
steps.explain: $150 − $130 = $20. A $20 gap is not a reason for a 390% loan.

steps.prompt: A payment plan on a medical bill can cost less than a payday loan.
steps.explain: Many billers will split a balance. Ask before you borrow.

steps.prompt: Which option puts the car at risk?
choices: A payment plan with the hospital
steps.explain: The title is the car.

steps.prompt: Put the short-on-cash options from first try to last resort.
items: Call the biller and ask for a plan
Pause spending and sell something unused
A small credit-union loan if you can get one
steps.explain: Ask, then cut, then a normal loan, then the expensive door.

lessons.title: Dev’s Pile-Up
lessons.summary: The plans were small. The week they landed was not.

story.title: Four small plans
story.body:
Dev used buy now, pay later four times in a month: **$20**, **$35**, **$15**, and **$40**. Each one looked fine alone. They all come out the same week.

He has **$80** in the account after gas. He also saw a payday ad: **$100** now, **$130** back in two weeks.

steps.prompt: How much do the four plans want in the same week?
He has $80 after gas. How much is he short?
The payday ad wants $130 back on $100. How much is that fee?
He takes the payday loan to cover the $30 gap. What is wrong with that fix?
choices: He pays a $30 fee to cover a $30 gap, and he still owes the $100
It pays off all four plans forever
steps.explain: A $30 fee to borrow the $30 he is short is a terrible trade. He would owe $130.

steps.prompt: One buy-now-pay-later plan is the same risk as four of them due the same week.
steps.explain: The stack is the problem. $110 is not $20.

steps.prompt: What is the better move this week?
choices: Pay what he can, ask one plan or biller for a few days, and do not open the payday loan
steps.explain: A short delay beats a two-week fee the size of the gap.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Payday, BNPL & Other Traps
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A $20 fee on a $100 loan, every two weeks, for a full year of 26 periods. What is the APR?
A title loan puts which asset on the line?
steps.explain: The title is the collateral.

steps.prompt: Four buy-now-pay-later plans due the same week cost the same as one of them.
steps.explain: Add the payments. They leave together.

steps.prompt: $45 a week for 80 weeks, versus a $500 cash price. How much more do the weekly payments cost?
